title: How to Make Arepas

lines.text: Hi, everyone! Today I'm showing you how to make arepas, a typical food from Colombia and Venezuela.
It's really easy. You only need four things.
Two cups of pre-cooked corn flour, two and a half cups of warm water, a teaspoon of salt, and a little butter.
First, put the flour and the salt in a big bowl.
Then add the warm water slowly and mix it with your hands.
After about two minutes, you have a soft dough. Now, leave it for five minutes.
Next, take a small ball of dough and make it flat, like a thick pancake.
Heat a pan with a little butter.
Cook each arepa for about six minutes on each side, until it's golden.
You can eat them with cheese, eggs, or avocado. My favourite is with white cheese. Enjoy!

title: Why Sleep Matters

lines.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome back to Healthy Habits. I'm Rachel.
And I'm Omar. Today, we're talking about something we all need but rarely get enough of: sleep.
Right. So Omar, how many hours do you usually sleep?
Honestly? About six. I know, I know, it's not enough.
Experts say adults need between seven and nine hours a night. Teenagers need even more, around nine or ten.
Wow. So what happens if we don't get enough?

Well, in the short term, you find it harder to concentrate and remember things. And you're more likely to feel stressed or irritable. Over time, poor sleep is linked to health problems like heart disease.
OK, that's a bit scary. So, what can we do?
The most important tip is to go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even at weekends.
Even on Saturdays? That's tough.
I know! Another tip is to avoid screens for at least an hour before bed. The light from phones tells your brain it's still daytime.
Guilty. I usually check my phone in bed.
And watch your coffee. Caffeine can stay in your body for up to six hours, so try not to drink it after about two in the afternoon.
What about naps? I love a nap.
Short naps are fine, about twenty minutes. Longer than that and you might wake up feeling worse.
Great advice. I'm going to try going phone-free tonight.
Let us know how it goes! Next week, we're talking about healthy snacks.

title: A Coffee Farmer from Huila

lines.text: Today on Global Kitchen, I'm talking to Luz Marina Cárdenas, a coffee farmer from Huila, in the south of Colombia. Welcome.
Thank you. It's a pleasure to be here.
Tell us a bit about your farm.
Well, it's a small family farm. My grandfather bought the land in nineteen sixty-five, and now my brother and I run it together. We have about eight hectares, at around seventeen hundred metres.
Why is altitude important for coffee?
At higher altitudes, the coffee cherries grow more slowly, and that gives them more flavour. Our coffee has notes of chocolate and orange.
Sounds delicious. What's a typical day like during the harvest?
We start very early, at about five in the morning. All the cherries are picked by hand, because they don't all ripen at the same time. During the harvest, we employ around twelve extra workers.
What are the biggest challenges for you?

Definitely the climate. The rain has become very unpredictable. Some years it rains too much, and the cherries fall before they're ready. Also, the price of coffee changes a lot, so it's hard to plan.
How are you dealing with that?
A few years ago, we started selling directly to small roasters in Canada and Japan. We get a fairer price, and they know exactly where the coffee comes from.
And what's your dream for the future?
I'd like to open a small café on the farm, so tourists can see the whole process, from the plant to the cup.
Luz Marina, thank you so much.

Finally, we'll finish on the second floor with an exhibition about how people lived here a hundred years ago.
There's a full-size kitchen from that time, and children love it, so watch out for school groups!
If you get lost, just look for someone in a blue jacket. All our staff wear them.
And please stay with the group when we're moving between floors, because the stairs can get crowded.
